title: Field-locked SIEM export patterns for multi-tenant environments and RBAC v2
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working playbook captures recommended patterns for shipping SIEM export payloads from Redwood Inference in multi-tenant environments while preserving RBAC v2 semantics, audit log fidelity, and evidence automation hooks. It focuses on Splunk/Datadog/Microsoft Sentinel integrations and customer-facing connector requirements.

Why this doc exists (context):
- Customers frequently require a tight mapping between tenant-aware RBAC decisions and fields emitted to their SIEMs for audit/evidence purposes.
- Export connectors must support field-level redaction/encryption, per-tenant routing, and evidence automation triggers (proof-of-delivery, retention hooks).
- We need a consistent test plan and a minimal interoperability envelope that works across Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC), Datadog logs intake, and Azure Sentinel connectors.

Design goals and constraints:
- Preserve audit integrity: every exported event should contain a small, consistent audit header that ties back to the RBAC decision, request id, and policy version.
- Tenant isolation: no cross-tenant PII leakage; allow customer-configurable safelists/denylists.
- Evidence automation compatibility: exported events must support deterministic hooks (evidence_id, evidence_stage, signature) so downstream automation can validate ingestion and retention.
- Backwards-compatible fallbacks: when a customer or connector does not support a field (e.g., encryption), fall back to hashed placeholders and annotate that a transformation was applied.

Minimal SIEM export envelope (canonical):
- top-level keys we require across all connectors: timestamp, tenant_id, request_id, actor_id, rbaced_role, policy_version, event_type, event_payload, evidence.{evidence_id,evidence_stage,signature}, export_version, transformation_applied

Example JSON (stringified - this is the minimal canonical structure we expect connectors to accept):

{
  "timestamp": "2025-07-12T19:23:44Z",
  "tenant_id": "t-8347f2",
  "request_id": "req-1a2b3c4d",
  "actor_id": "user:alice@example.com",
  "rbaced_role": "platform:read-only",
  "policy_version": "rbac-v2@2025-06-10",
  "event_type": "model.inference.generated",
  "event_payload": {
    "model": "redwood-compact-13b",
    "input_tokens_count": 142,
    "output_tokens_count": 63
  },
  "evidence": {
    "evidence_id": "ev-20250712-72c9",
    "evidence_stage": "exported-to-siem",
    "signature": "sha256:9f2d..."
  },
  "export_version": "1.0-field-locked",
  "transformation_applied": "none"
}

Field-level handling recommendations:
- PII fields (email, IPs, user-provided content) should be redacted by default for Shared (hosted) customers. Allow tenant opt-in to include hashed or plaintext values according to contract.
- Field encryption: if a customer requests field-level encryption, connectors MUST carry a header: encryption_scheme and key_id. When encryption is applied, include a metadata placeholder with the SHA256 of the plaintext and a note of the kms provider (e.g., AWS-KMS, GCP-KMS, HSM-vendor).
- Transformation annotation: any transformation (redaction, truncation, hashing, encryption) must be recorded in transformation_applied. Example values: none | redacted(email) | hashed(user_text) | encrypted(audit_blob:kms:aws-us-east-1:key/abc).

RBAC v2 mapping pattern (how to map RBAC to exported fields):
- rbaced_role: canonical short role (platform:admin, tenant:admin, tenant:writer, platform:svcaccount).
- policy_version: the semantic tag for the RBAC policy set used to make the decision (git tag or timestamped policy id).
- decision_evidence: a compressed tag representing why the decision was made (optional for low-volume customers). Use Decision IDs for later retrieval (e.g., dec-98bca).

Example RBAC header notes (text):
- Keep the RBAC header minimal to avoid leaking scope. The tenant_id and rbaced_role are sufficient for most SIEM detection rules.
- For high-assurance audits the connector can include a signed policy snapshot URL in the signature field of evidence so auditors can validate rule text.

Connector-specific guidance (Splunk / Datadog / Sentinel):
- Splunk HEC:
  - Use bulk batching (size cap ~1000 events or 5MB) for high-throughput tenants; prefer ingestion through HEC tokens scoped per-tenant.
  - Include X-Splunk-Request-Id header mapped to request_id.
  - For encrypted fields, use event.encrypted = true and provide encryption metadata under event.metadata.encryption.
- Datadog Logs:
  - Use JSON logs ingestion; map tenant_id -> attributes.tenant_id and rbaced_role -> attributes.rbac.role.
  - Use Datadog facets to index tenant_id and policy_version for fast search.
  - Streams must include the evidence.signature string in a fixed attribute name dd.evidence.signature to enable automated monitors.
- Azure Sentinel (Event Hub/Log Analytics Connector):
  - Use JSON flattening conventions expected by the Log Analytics schema; keep the evidence.* fields at top-level to avoid schema drift.
  - When using Event Hub as transport, set partition key to tenant_id to preserve ordering per-tenant.

Customer requirements checklist (for onboarding):
1) Desired retention window for SIEM exports (default 90 days for host-level telemetry)
2) PII policy: allowlist/denylist or encryption requirement
3) RBAC evidence depth: minimal (tenant_id + role) vs. full decision logs
4) Ingestion endpoints and credentials (HEC tokens, Datadog API keys, Event Hub connection strings)
5) Throughput expectations (peak RPS, average tokens/sec, burst tolerance)
6) SLA for delivery and proof-of-delivery requirements (webhook ack, evidence receipts)
7) Regulatory constraints (e.g., EU data residency, GDPR special handling)
8) Auditability requirements (signed snapshots, policy retention, signature verification process)

Operational requirements and failure modes:
- Backpressure: if SIEM endpoint responds 429/503, connector must buffer up to tenant-configured retention (default 1 hour) and send transformed events with transformation_applied set to "backpressure-buffered".
- Partial success: if a batch partially succeeds, emit a companion control event: type=export.control.batch_result with counts {sent, failed, transformed} and include evidence_id for correlation.
- Data-loss mitigation: if buffer overflows, mark affected events with transformation_applied="dropped:overflow" and generate a high-severity paging alert with list of sample request_ids.

Evidence automation hooks (how SIEM consumers validate export integrity):
- Proof-of-delivery receipts: connectors should request or generate an ingestion receipt (id and timestamp) from the SIEM when supported; store mapping of evidence_id -> ingestion_receipt.
- Periodic verification: nightly job that replays a signed summary of exported evidence_ids to the customer (or their auditor), signed by Redwood's export key.
- Signature scheme: use SHA256 over canonicalized JSON + export_version + kms_key_id; provide verification instructions and the public key in the customer onboarding artifact.

Test plan and acceptance criteria (for integration engineering):
- Unit tests: redaction and encryption transformations for 30 example payloads across three tenant types.
- Integration tests: send 10k synthetic events in 10-second bursts to each connector (Splunk/Datadog/Sentinel) and assert: all events return success or proper retry/backpressure behavior, no PII leaks when tenant is default-redaction, evidence receipts are stored.
- Compliance tests: verify policy_version included and that a signed policy snapshot is retrievable for any evidence_id listed in a 30-day period.

Sample onboarding template (what we request from customer):
- Ingestion endpoints + preferred transport
- Retention and legal constraints
- Encryption preferences and KMS details
- RBAC evidence depth choice: minimal | standard | full-decision-logs
- Test window: preferred date/time, expected throughput in TPS

Open questions and design tradeoffs (notes to reviewers):
- Do we require connectors to support signed receipts from all SIEMs? Some providers (Datadog) do not provide strong receipts; fallback will be Redwood-signed ingestion events.
- Should policy snapshots be stored for longer than the default export retention? Pro: auditors need them; Con: storage cost and potential policy leakage.
- Multi-tenant ordering guarantees vs throughput: partitioning by tenant gives ordering but reduces batching efficiency.

Appendix: quick glossary of fields (one-line):
- tenant_id: canonical tenant identifier
- request_id: unique id per API request/operation
- rbaced_role: short canonical role used in decision
- policy_version: policy tag used for decision
- evidence_id: unique id to track an exported event across systems
- evidence.signature: SHA256 or KMS-signed token proving origin

Next steps (immediate):
- Feedback requested from eng-observability and platform-network on batching/fallback choices (owner: Morgan Lee)
- Prototype connector changes to include transformation_applied and evidence receipts (owner: Riley Patel)
- Add integration test skeleton to telemetry repo (linked PR above)

Notes to file owner:
- This is a working doc. Keep the minimal envelope stable; changes require cross-team sign-off (security, privacy, SRE).
- Tag any schema evolution with an export_version bump (semantic: major.minor-purpose).

End of playbook (working draft).
